sentences.text: The Global Nonviolent Action Database, known as GNAD, is a "database of case studies of nonviolent action campaigns, browsable by case, tag, method and map" (maryleelabor record), which its home page calls "a project of Swarthmore College, including the Peace and Conflict Studies Program, the Peace Collection, and the Lang Center for Civic and Social Responsibility", under the line "Powering Learning about Nonviolent Action" (home page).

CNCR describes it as "A database of over 1000 summaries of nonviolent campaigns worldwide", the Swarthmore Peace & Conflict Studies blog as one that "presents cases of nonviolent civil resistance from around the world, spanning decades and even hundreds of years", the Discuss Data review as reporting "on cases of nonviolent protest actions taken across the globe", and the Policy Commons card as providing "access to information about hundreds of cases of nonviolent action" (CNCR; the blog; Discuss Data review, 2025; Policy Commons card).

The maryleelabor census, anchored on #1725, asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", and enters it under labor action with "case record" as its kind of evidence (maryleelabor record).

Its unit is the campaign: the home page's menu carries a page titled "Campaigns, Not Movements", and CNCR states the rule, "the case studies included are indeed, campaigns, and not movements. For example, “the civil rights movement” is not included, but the Montgomery Bus Boycott is a case", which CNCR's card gives as "excluding broad moveme..." and the census records as "a case: a nonviolent action campaign (a menu page is titled 'Campaigns, Not Movements'), linked to the methods it used" (home page; CNCR; maryleelabor record).

Each case "is presented in two formats: the database file (with searchable fields) and the narrative describing the struggle as an unfolding story" (CNCR), beside "a more visual representation in the form of an interactive map" (Discuss Data review), and the encyclopedia's account says it "includes a narrative for each case" (Wikipedia, George Lakey).

Its case map has a "Filter by Wave of Campaign" running from "Latin American Democracy Campaigns (1944)" to "Arab Awakening (2011)", each case on the map carrying its "Campaign Wave" (case map), and "by pressing each “wave” button one can find cases" (CNCR).

The archive reads "the case as the unit that carries a campaign's course in prose, which an event count does not", and the census keeps the database apart as "NOT a database of movements: its unit is the campaign" and "NOT an event count" (maryleelabor record).

#1725 states what a case record shows that a measure of conflict does not: the charge that the left infights "measures how much conflict there is", and "At the level of mechanics the case record tells a different story. Disagreement is constant. What varies is the ending, and the endings fall into a small number of forms" (#1725).

It states the case record's limit with it: "no cross-organization dataset of left splits, or of minority positions later adopted, was found for any period", and the pattern's "frequency across the left as a whole is unmeasured" (#1725); of this database the census writes that it does not answer "the frequency of nonviolent action in any country or period (the cases are written up one by one)" (maryleelabor record).

Its home page counts "1,200+ cases", "100+ countries" and "400+ years covered", which the census, reading the home page on 31 October 2026, takes as its count, its coverage and its holdings (home page; maryleelabor record).

Other counts differ: the Discuss Data review gives "1.300+ total entries", "40 events" of them for Eastern Europe, the South Caucasus and Central Asia, the encyclopedia "over 1,000 researched cases from nearly 200 countries", and CNCR cases "drawn from all continents and most countries" (Discuss Data review, 2025; Wikipedia, George Lakey; CNCR).
Its range runs from "a case from ancient Egypt, 12th century BCE" (CNCR) to cases "all the way up to 2019" (Discuss Data review, citing Lakey 2011a).

It researches "campaigns that have reached a point of completion" (CNCR, in the database's own first person), and the CNCR card calls its cases "completed nonviolent campaign case studies" (card snippet).

"Each campaign is sorted in one (or several) issue “clusters”", and the cases show people "struggling for human rights, economic justice, democracy, national and ethnic identity, environmental sustainability, and peace" (CNCR).

Its definition of nonviolent action, as the Discuss Data review quotes Lakey (2011c), is "[A] technique of struggle that goes beyond institutionalized conflict procedures like law courts and voting", the study of "the methods of protest, noncooperation, and intervention that typically heighten a conflict", which "is not located in the discourse of morality and ethics" and focuses "descriptively on what people do when they use this specific ‘technique of struggle.’"

Its summaries are researched to "provide free access to information about hundreds of cases of nonviolent action for learning and for citizen action" and to "make available comparative information that will support researchers and writers to develop strategic knowledge and theory" (CNCR).

It has been "A project of Swarthmore College, 2011-present" (CNCR); Wikipedia has no article under its name, which redirects to George Lakey, an activist and sociologist "who added academic underpinning to the concept of nonviolent revolution", whose article lists it among his works as "Developed by Lakey with Swarthmore College and other university students" (Wikipedia, George Lakey).

Students write its cases: "Seventy-six new cases have been added to the Global Nonviolent Action Database by students in the spring semester Strategy and Nonviolent Struggle course at Swarthmore College" (the blog, 2015), a course that "is a research seminar and writing course that contributes to the widely recognized Global Nonviolent Action Database" (the blog, 2017).

Lakey's article cites the database's cases for campaigns he took part in, "Puerto Ricans expel United States Navy from Culebra Island, 1970–1974" and "Earth Quaker Action Team Campaigns Against PNC Bank for Financing Mountaintop Removal Coal Mining 2010–2015" among them (Wikipedia, George Lakey).

The census enters it under labor action, "strikes, stoppages and protest events, counted and described", tags it "NOT a labor dataset: labor cases are one part of a database of nonviolent action of every kind", and names among its featured cases "a labor strike (Guatemalan workers at Lunafil)" (maryleelabor record); the home page features "Guatemalan workers at Lunafil strike" and "Macalester students stage sit-in to oppose sweatshop apparel, 2000", and the case map's waves include the "Student Anti-Sweatshop Labor Movement (1990s - 2010s)" and the "Student Living Wage Movement (late 1990s - mid 2000s)" (home page; case map).

The archive defines its semantic strike against the class these labor cases belong to: in the "Conventional work stoppage" what stops is "Production", who acts is "Workers against an employer", the success condition is "Concession from management", and it ends when "Demands met" (#1438).

It reads the general strike of the enslaved, through Du Bois, in its own terms of noun and verb: "The general strike is the verb withdrawn from the noun's owner. The workers reorganized the topology themselves, by moving", and "The freedpeople's own general strike forced the opening; the settlement closed it toward contract and debt" (#1668).

The home page licenses it "under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International license unless otherwise noted", and the census records its holder as "Swarthmore College; licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 unless otherwise noted; the public can suggest a case", its license as stated, and what it keeps as "the record of nonviolent campaigns, written up as cases" (home page; maryleelabor record).

Its menu offers "Browse Cases", "Browse Cases by Tags", "View Cases on Map", "Browse Methods" and "Suggest a Case", and "Registered users can login to the website" (home page), which the census records as "public browse and search of cases, tags, methods and map" (maryleelabor record); the Discuss Data review adds that "while the data is freely viewable on the website, it seems that the data is not available for download".

#1725 names the decisive variable in a record of disputes as "what happens to the losing position after the decision", whether the defeated critique kept "an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it" (#1725).

For this database the census records the losing side as "not recorded. A 'Limitations of the Database' page and coding definitions are listed and were not read; the saved pages do not show whether failed campaigns or splits inside campaigns are recorded", its stated limits as that page, and its method as "written case studies coded against definitions" (maryleelabor record), the home page listing "Limitations of the Database", "Coding Definitions" and "Who Made the Database?" (home page).

The Discuss Data review of Nathalie Rathkamp (version 1.0, "published: May 8, 2025") lists its methods of data collection as "Desk Research", "Event Data" and "Text Coding"; the census writes that its record settles "how a named nonviolent campaign was conducted, as the case writes it up" and leaves "strikes or campaigns that have no case" and "the positions argued inside a campaign (not shown in the saved pages)" unsettled (Discuss Data review; maryleelabor record).

The census records it "active": "the site answered on 2026-10-31 and takes case suggestions; update dates are not recorded in the saved text", and lists as unchecked "the cases themselves" and "how many cases concern labor" (maryleelabor record); the Discuss Data review wrote that "As of summer 2024, it is not clear whether work on the data collection is continuing", and the blog tags it on events such as "Animating Resistance: Live Cinema Explorations of the Global Nonviolent Action Database" (Discuss Data review; the blog).

At its name, a new address ("the census name; NEW address."), the Overview of 31 October 2026, signed out, gives "its host, its scale, its clusters and how to search it", and the Capture Registry reads it "Faithful on host and scale", with "Swarthmore named; the database's pages among the cards" and "The database reached by name with its host, scope, clusters and tools" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The Capture Registry finds "'400 YEARS' AND 'ANCIENT EGYPT' IN ONE SENTENCE", the rule "'Campaigns, Not Movements' reaches the composition only through a card snippet", and that "The database links a page of its own 'Limitations of the Database' and a Creative Commons license (BY-NC-ND 4.0); the composition carries neither": the composition "leaves out the database's own statement of its unit, limits and license" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

sentences.text: The Global Nonviolent Action Database is a project of Swarthmore College with its Peace and Conflict Studies Program, the Peace Collection and the Lang Center, under the line "Powering Learning about Nonviolent Action" (home page).

It is a database of summaries of nonviolent campaigns worldwide (CNCR), of cases of nonviolent civil resistance in narrative form (the Swarthmore blog) and of nonviolent protest actions across the globe (Discuss Data), with information on hundreds of cases (Policy Commons card).
Its cases are campaigns and exclude movements: the civil rights movement is no case, the Montgomery Bus Boycott is one (CNCR; the home page's menu; the CNCR card).
Each case is a database file with searchable fields and a narrative of the struggle, beside an interactive map (CNCR; Discuss Data; Wikipedia).
The case map groups cases into twelve waves of campaigns, from the Latin American democracy campaigns of 1944 to the Arab Awakening of 2011 (case map; CNCR).

It counts 1,200+ cases, 100+ countries and 400+ years (home page), the review 1.300+ entries and the encyclopedia over 1,000 cases from nearly 200 countries, drawn from all continents (Discuss Data; Wikipedia; CNCR).
Its cases run from ancient Egypt in the 12th century BCE to 2019, and it researches campaigns that have reached completion (CNCR; Discuss Data).
Campaigns are sorted into six issue clusters: democracy, economic justice, environment, human rights, national and ethnic identity, and peace (CNCR).
Lakey's definition, which the review quotes, takes nonviolent action as a technique of struggle beyond courts and voting, described apart from morality and ethics (Discuss Data).
It aims at free access for learning and citizen action and at comparative knowledge for researchers and writers (CNCR).

Begun in 2011 and developed by George Lakey with students, to whose article its Wikipedia title redirects, it gains cases from the Strategy and Nonviolent Struggle course, and Lakey's article cites its cases for his own campaigns (CNCR; Wikipedia; the blog).
Its labor cases include the Lunafil strike and the waves of the student anti-sweatshop and living-wage movements (home page; case map).

It is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and browsable by case, tag, map and method, with case suggestions and logins; its data can be viewed and, it seems to the review, cannot be downloaded (home page; Discuss Data).

It lists limitations and coding pages; the 2025 review records desk research, event data and text coding, and found it unclear in 2024 whether collection continues, while the blog shows the database in use (home page; Discuss Data; the blog).

Each case "is presented in two formats: the database file (with searchable fields) and the narrative describing the struggle as an unfolding story" (CNCR), beside "a more visual representation in the form of an interactive map" (Discuss Data review), and the encyclopedia's account says it "includes a narrative for each case" (Wikipedia, George Lakey). Its case map has a "Filter by Wave of Campaign" running from "Latin American Democracy Campaigns (1944)" to "Arab Awakening (2011)", each case on the map carrying its "Campaign Wave" (case map), and "by pressing each “wave” button one can find cases" (CNCR). The archive reads "the case as the unit that carries a campaign's course in prose, which an event count does not", and the census keeps the database apart as "NOT a database of movements: its unit is the campaign" and "NOT an event count" (maryleelabor record). #1725 states what a case record shows that a measure of conflict does not: the charge that the left infights "measures how much conflict there is", and "At the level of mechanics the case record tells a different story. Disagreement is constant. What varies is the ending, and the endings fall into a small number of forms" (#1725). It states the case record's limit with it: "no cross-organization dataset of left splits, or of minority positions later adopted, was found for any period", and the pattern's "frequency across the left as a whole is unmeasured" (#1725); of this database the census writes that it does not answer "the frequency of nonviolent action in any country or period (the cases are written up one by one)" (maryleelabor record). Its home page counts "1,200+ cases", "100+ countries" and "400+ years covered", which the census, reading the home page on 31 October 2026, takes as its count, its coverage and its holdings (home page; maryleelabor record). Other counts differ: the Discuss Data review gives "1.300+ total entries", "40 events" of them for Eastern Europe, the South Caucasus and Central Asia, the encyclopedia "over 1,000 researched cases from nearly 200 countries", and CNCR cases "drawn from all continents and most countries" (Discuss Data review, 2025; Wikipedia, George Lakey; CNCR). Its range runs from "a case from ancient Egypt, 12th century BCE" (CNCR) to cases "all the way up to 2019" (Discuss Data review, citing Lakey 2011a). It researches "campaigns that have reached a point of completion" (CNCR, in the database's own first person), and the CNCR card calls its cases "completed nonviolent campaign case studies" (card snippet). "Each campaign is sorted in one (or several) issue “clusters”", and the cases show people "struggling for human rights, economic justice, democracy, national and ethnic identity, environmental sustainability, and peace" (CNCR). Its definition of nonviolent action, as the Discuss Data review quotes Lakey (2011c), is "[A] technique of struggle that goes beyond institutionalized conflict procedures like law courts and voting", the study of "the methods of protest, noncooperation, and intervention that typically heighten a conflict", which "is not located in the discourse of morality and ethics" and focuses "descriptively on what people do when they use this specific ‘technique of struggle.’" Its summaries are researched to "provide free access to information about hundreds of cases of nonviolent action for learning and for citizen action" and to "make available comparative information that will support researchers and writers to develop strategic knowledge and theory" (CNCR). It has been "A project of Swarthmore College, 2011-present" (CNCR); Wikipedia has no article under its name, which redirects to George Lakey, an activist and sociologist "who added academic underpinning to the concept of nonviolent revolution", whose article lists it among his works as "Developed by Lakey with Swarthmore College and other university students" (Wikipedia, George Lakey). Students write its cases: "Seventy-six new cases have been added to the Global Nonviolent Action Database by students in the spring semester Strategy and Nonviolent Struggle course at Swarthmore College" (the blog, 2015), a course that "is a research seminar and writing course that contributes to the widely recognized Global Nonviolent Action Database" (the blog, 2017). Lakey's article cites the database's cases for campaigns he took part in, "Puerto Ricans expel United States Navy from Culebra Island, 1970–1974" and "Earth Quaker Action Team Campaigns Against PNC Bank for Financing Mountaintop Removal Coal Mining 2010–2015" among them (Wikipedia, George Lakey). The census enters it under labor action, "strikes, stoppages and protest events, counted and described", tags it "NOT a labor dataset: labor cases are one part of a database of nonviolent action of every kind", and names among its featured cases "a labor strike (Guatemalan workers at Lunafil)" (maryleelabor record); the home page features "Guatemalan workers at Lunafil strike" and "Macalester students stage sit-in to oppose sweatshop apparel, 2000", and the case map's waves include the "Student Anti-Sweatshop Labor Movement (1990s - 2010s)" and the "Student Living Wage Movement (late 1990s - mid 2000s)" (home page; case map). The archive defines its semantic strike against the class these labor cases belong to: in the "Conventional work stoppage" what stops is "Production", who acts is "Workers against an employer", the success condition is "Concession from management", and it ends when "Demands met" (#1438). It reads the general strike of the enslaved, through Du Bois, in its own terms of noun and verb: "The general strike is the verb withdrawn from the noun's owner. The workers reorganized the topology themselves, by moving", and "The freedpeople's own general strike forced the opening; the settlement closed it toward contract and debt" (#1668). The home page licenses it "under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International license unless otherwise noted", and the census records its holder as "Swarthmore College; licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 unless otherwise noted; the public can suggest a case", its license as stated, and what it keeps as "the record of nonviolent campaigns, written up as cases" (home page; maryleelabor record). Its menu offers "Browse Cases", "Browse Cases by Tags", "View Cases on Map", "Browse Methods" and "Suggest a Case", and "Registered users can login to the website" (home page), which the census records as "public browse and search of cases, tags, methods and map" (maryleelabor record); the Discuss Data review adds that "while the data is freely viewable on the website, it seems that the data is not available for download". #1725 names the decisive variable in a record of disputes as "what happens to the losing position after the decision", whether the defeated critique kept "an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it" (#1725). For this database the census records the losing side as "not recorded. A 'Limitations of the Database' page and coding definitions are listed and were not read; the saved pages do not show whether failed campaigns or splits inside campaigns are recorded", its stated limits as that page, and its method as "written case studies coded against definitions" (maryleelabor record), the home page listing "Limitations of the Database", "Coding Definitions" and "Who Made the Database?" (home page). The Discuss Data review of Nathalie Rathkamp (version 1.0, "published: May 8, 2025") lists its methods of data collection as "Desk Research", "Event Data" and "Text Coding"; the census writes that its record settles "how a named nonviolent campaign was conducted, as the case writes it up" and leaves "strikes or campaigns that have no case" and "the positions argued inside a campaign (not shown in the saved pages)" unsettled (Discuss Data review; maryleelabor record).
